text: More than 3,000 years ago, the Olmecs lived in hot, wet lowlands by the Gulf of Mexico.
Their town of San Lorenzo, on high ground above a river, became the region’s largest.
src: The Olmecs built the first great centres of Mesoamerica, San Lorenzo and then La Venta, in the tropical lowlands of Mexico’s Gulf Coast between about 1200 and 400 BCE / The Olmec heartland lies in the hot, wet lowlands along the southern Gulf of Mexico

San Lorenzo itself, on a plateau that rises some 50 metres above the floodplain of the Coatzacoalcos / c. 1200 BCE: San Lorenzo, above the Coatzacoalcos river, becomes the largest centre in Mesoamerica

text: Farmers grew maize, beans and squash, and people fished and hunted deer.
One of their pots held traces of cacao, the plant chocolate is made from.
src: Farmers grew maize, which became more important over the centuries, together with beans and squash, and they fished, hunted deer
Traces of cacao on a pot from El Manatí of about 1750 BCE are among the earliest evidence in Mesoamerica for the use of the plant from which chocolate is made

text: Sculptors carved seventeen giant stone heads, each with its own face and headdress.
They probably show rulers, and their stone was moved many kilometres from a volcano.
src: Seventeen colossal heads are known / Each head has its own face and headdress

The colossal heads, each with its own features and headdress, are usually seen as portraits of individual rulers / most were carved from basalt of Cerro Cintepec, a volcano in the Tuxtla Mountains, which had to be moved across many kilometres / the transport of monuments weighing many tonnes without draught animals or wheels

text: They made the oldest known rubber balls, from the sap of the rubber tree.
They may have used them to play a ball game.
src: the oldest known rubber balls / people in the region were making rubber from the latex of the rubber tree
and perhaps playing the ballgame, by about 1600 BCE

text: Later, La Venta became their main centre, with an earth pyramid 34 metres high.
Its people buried great offerings of stone that were never meant to be seen again.
src: c. 900 BCE: San Lorenzo declines, and La Venta in Tabasco becomes the leading Olmec centre / rose an earthen pyramid 34 metres high
At La Venta people also buried great offerings that were never meant to be seen again. One held some 50 tonnes of finished serpentine blocks

text: Olmec art spread far across the land, to places such as San José Mogote.
La Venta was left about 2,400 years ago, but their images of rulers and gods lived on in Maya art.
src: Objects and images in the Olmec style appear far beyond the Gulf Coast / at San José Mogote in the Valley of Oaxaca
c. 400 BCE: La Venta is abandoned / Their images of rulers, gods and the cosmos spread across Mesoamerica and helped shape the art and religion of later peoples such as the Maya
